The magnetic force is the centripetal force, 𝑟= 𝑚𝑣/ (𝑒𝐵). The force is perpendicular to → 𝐵 but does not act on motion along → 𝐵.

items.title: Get It? (Thomson's experiment): In a velocity selector, electrons are pushed upward by the electric force, and the magnetic force on them is downward but weaker, so the beam curves upward. How could you change the magnetic field so the beam travels straight?

items.title: 27 (Lesson 3, Challenge): An electron moves in a magnetic field that decreases linearly with time. Describe its path

body.html: The radius of a circular path is 𝑟= 𝑚𝑣/ (𝑒𝐵). The magnetic force does no work, so the speed stays (nearly) constant. As 𝐵 falls, 𝑟 grows.

As 𝐵 decreases, 𝑟∝1 / 𝐵 increases: for example, when 𝐵 has fallen to one fourth of its starting value, 𝑟 is four times as large. The electron starts on a circle and bends less and less sharply, curving in the sense appropriate for a negative charge (opposite to a positive ion). The path does not close; it is an outward spiral. (A changing 𝐵 also induces a circulating electric field that changes the speed slightly, but the main result is the widening spiral.)

answer.html: The electron follows a spiral that opens outward (radius growing roughly as 1 / 𝐵), turning in the sense opposite to that of a positive charge.

check.html: If 𝐵 were constant, 𝑟 would be constant and the path would be a circle.

items.title: 31 (Lesson 3, Challenge): Thomson could remove at most two electrons from a helium atom. What could he conclude about the positive charge left behind?

answer.html: A helium atom is neutral, so the positive charge left after two electrons are removed equals the charge of those two electrons, +2𝑒= + 3.204 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>19</sup> C. items.title: Focus Question: How does a mass spectrometer work?

answer.html: Atoms are ionized (electrons knocked off), accelerated by an electric potential difference to a known kinetic energy, and sent into a uniform magnetic field. The field bends the ions into circles of radius 𝑟=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sup>𝐵</sup>√2𝑉<sup>accel</sup>𝑚/ 𝑞, so heavier ions travel on larger circles. The landing position on a detector gives 𝑟, and then 𝑞/ 𝑚= 2𝑉<sub>accel</sub> / (𝐵<sup>2</sup>𝑟<sup>2</sup>) gives each ion's mass.

items.title: 27 (Lesson 3, Challenge): Path of a positive ion in a magnetic field that increases linearly with time

body.html: The radius of a circular path is 𝑟= 𝑚𝑣/ (𝑞𝐵). The magnetic force does no work, so the ion's speed stays (nearly) constant while the field grows, so 𝑟∝1 / 𝐵 gets smaller.

As 𝐵 grows linearly with time, 𝑟= 𝑚𝑣/ (𝑞𝐵) falls like 1 / 𝑡. The ion therefore starts on a circle and curves more and more tightly, in the sense a positive charge turns (opposite to an electron). It does not close into a circle; it follows an inward spiral toward a point. (A changing 𝐵 also induces a circulating electric field, which does a small amount of work on the ion and changes its speed. That is the idea behind the betatron, but the main result is the tightening spiral.)

answer.html: The ion follows a spiral that tightens inward (radius decreasing roughly as 1 / 𝐵), turning in the direction appropriate for a positive charge.

check.html: Limiting case: if 𝐵 were constant, 𝑟 would be constant and the path would be a circle.

items.title: 31 (Lesson 3, Challenge): Thomson could never remove more than one electron from a hydrogen atom. What could he conclude about its positive charge?

answer.html: A hydrogen atom is neutral, so the positive charge that remains after one electron is removed equals that electron's charge, +𝑒. If the atom had a larger positive charge it would have more electrons to remove. Since he could remove only one, he could conclude that a hydrogen atom has only one unit (+𝑒) of positive charge, with just one electron to balance it.

check.html: Matches the modern picture of one proton and one electron.

items.title: Figure 20: Calculate the average mass of the chromium isotopes

body.html: From Figure 20 the isotopes are at 50 (4.345 %), 52 (83.789 %), 53 (9.501 %), and 54 (2.365 %). The percentages add to 100 %. (The figure shows 83.789 % for mass 52; the image text says 87.789, but 83.789 is the value that makes the total 100.)
The average mass is the weighted average of the isotope masses, each multiplied by its fractional abundance.

items.title: spectrometer separates ions of different masses

answer.html: If all the ions have the same charge 𝑞, the same accelerating potential difference 𝑉<sub>accel</sub>, and the same field 𝐵, then 𝑟 depends only on the mass: 𝑟∝√𝑚. Heavier ions are harder to turn and travel on larger circles, and lighter ions on smaller ones. They therefore strike the detector at different distances from the slit, and the distance (twice the radius) identifies each mass.

check.html: Quadrupling the mass doubles the radius.

items.title: 33 (Check Your Progress): How does Thomson's cathode-ray tube form an electron beam?

answer.html: Nearly all the air is pumped out of a glass tube, and a large potential difference is applied between the cathode (negative) and the anodes. Negatively charged particles are pulled from the atoms of the tiny amount of remaining gas and accelerated from the cathode toward the anodes. Slits in the anodes let only a narrow stream through, forming a beam that travels to the far end, where it makes a glowing spot on the fluorescent coating.

check.html: The beam's presence is shown by the spot on the screen.

items.title: 34 (Check Your Progress): How must the magnetic field change for ions with hundreds of proton masses, using the same accelerating potential difference?

body.html: 𝑟=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup>
<sup>𝑞</sup>. To hit the same detector spot, keep 𝑟 the same, so 𝐵∝√𝑚 for fixed 𝑉 and 𝑞.
If the ion's mass is 𝑁 times larger, 𝐵 must be √𝑁 times larger. For example, ions 100 times heavier need √100 = 10 times the field.

answer.html: The magnetic field must be increased, in proportion to the square root of the ions' mass (for example, about 10 times stronger for ions 100 times heavier). Otherwise the heavy ions would travel in much larger circles and miss the detector.

check.html: Heavier ions bend less, so a stronger field is needed.
